lesson.title: Systematic Sampling: Every Kth Item on the List
lesson.summary: A systematic sample selects individuals from an ordered list at a fixed interval, choosing a random starting point and then taking every kth item, a method that approximates a simple random sample when the list has no hidden pattern.
lesson.body:
A systematic sample builds a sample from an ordered list using a fixed rule rather than drawing purely random selections one at a time. The procedure is straightforward: decide on an interval, k, pick a starting point at random from the first k items on the list, and then take every kth item after that starting point all the way through the list. If a factory produces 10,000 units per day and a quality inspector wants a sample of 100, the inspector could set k equal to 100, randomly pick a starting item somewhere in the first 100 produced, and then pull every hundredth unit off the line afterward.

Systematic sampling shares a family resemblance with simple random sampling in that it can, under the right conditions, give every individual on the list a known and equal chance of appearing in the sample, and it is often used as a practical stand-in when drawing a true simple random sample would be slow or awkward, for instance when there is no numbered master list to draw random index numbers from, but there is a physical or logical sequence, a line of people, a shelf of files, a conveyor belt, that can be walked through in order. The random starting point is what keeps the method from being fully deterministic and gives it its claim to being a form of random sampling rather than a convenience sample.

The one serious danger in systematic sampling is a hidden periodic pattern in the list that happens to line up with the chosen interval k. If a factory's production line has a defect that recurs every 20th unit because of a machine cycle, and the inspector happens to sample every 20th unit, the sample could wildly overrepresent or completely miss the defect, giving a badly distorted picture of overall quality. This is the main way a systematic sample can fail to behave like a simple random sample: it is not that individuals lack an equal chance in principle, it is that the fixed spacing can accidentally synchronize with real structure in the population.

Consider a hypothetical worked example. A researcher wants to sample 50 names from an alphabetized list of 1,000 city employees to survey about commute times. Since 1,000 divided by 50 is 20, the researcher sets k equal to 20, randomly selects a starting point between 1 and 20, say position 14, and then samples positions 14, 34, 54, 74, and so on up through position 994, yielding exactly 50 employees. Because an alphabetized list of last names has no plausible relationship to commute time, this systematic sample should behave essentially like a simple random sample for this particular question, giving a reasonably representative cross-section of commuters without needing a random number generator to draw 50 individual index numbers.

The practical appeal of systematic sampling is speed and simplicity, especially for large lists or physical sequences where generating and cross-referencing fifty or a hundred independent random numbers would be cumbersome. Its validity rests entirely on the assumption that the list's order carries no hidden cyclical relationship to the trait being measured; when that assumption holds, as it usually does for alphabetized rosters or arbitrarily ordered inventories, systematic sampling is a reasonable and efficient alternative to a full simple random sample.
